summary:
Across the 5 evals in this run, 3 involved substantive scored comparisons (serverless-review-methodology, silent-failure-correlation, evidence-and-scope-discipline), and 2 (rds-review-belongs-to-another-skill, unrelated-conceptual-question) were skipped entirely because they were "should_trigger: false" tests — for these, only trigger_fired was measured (both variants correctly triggered/did not trigger 3/3), and no expected-output, assertion, metric, or consistency data exists; they should be treated as absent, not as either variant failing.

For the three scored evals, a consistent and fairly large pattern appears: with_skill met the expected output in all 3/3 runs on all three evals, while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs on two evals and only partially benefited on the third via individual assertions. At the assertion level, with_skill passed at very high rates (92%, 100%, 100% across the three evals) with high average confidence on almost all LLM-judged assertions, while without_skill passed at much lower rates (12%, 0%, 28%). Many individual assertions follow a clean 'with_skill passes, without_skill fails' pattern — covering things like disclosing scope/limitations, citing severity, citing check identifiers, and separating verified vs. unverified findings. A couple of assertions were flaky for with_skill (e.g., the "no serverless resources, say so plainly" assertion passed only 1/3 with low confidence, and a cost-estimate-disclosure assertion was flaky for without_skill). One assertion (no raw 12-digit account IDs exposed) passed 3/3 for both variants in two evals — this assertion isn't distinguishing the two variants at all, since both handle it well.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) also favored with_skill in two of the three evals (mostly_consistent vs. inconsistent), while in the third (evidence-and-scope-discipline) both were rated mostly_consistent, with with_skill scoring marginally higher (2.5 vs 2.0) and both evaluated at only medium confidence.

On cost and runtime, without_skill was consistently faster and cheaper than with_skill by a substantial margin in all three evals (e.g., ~1m28s/$0.73 vs ~6m52s/$3.43; ~2m36s/$1.30 vs ~5m35s/$2.79; ~5m20s/$2.66 vs ~9m25s/$4.69), and also used noticeably less context window (roughly 5% vs 17–19% utilization). No quality-comparison pairs could be directly evaluated in any eval (all marked as skipped/0 pairs evaluated), so there is no separate head-to-head quality-judgment signal beyond the assertion and expected-output pass rates.

Taken together, the state of the data shows a clear tradeoff on the evals where comparison was possible: with_skill met expected outputs and individual assertions far more often and showed more run-to-run consistency, while without_skill was substantially faster, cheaper, and lighter on context usage. Confidence in the per-assertion LLM judgments is generally high, though a few specific assertions (the "no serverless resources" check, and the cost-estimate-disclosure check) carry lower confidence and flakiness and should be read more cautiously. No data exists to assess the two trigger-skipped evals beyond confirming correct trigger behavior for both variants.

serverless-review-methodology.summary:
This single chat-task eval compared with_skill and without_skill on a serverless-review style task. The behavior under test ("trigger") fired reliably for both variants (3/3).

Expected-output match showed a stark, high-confidence split: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, high confidence), while without_skill met it in none (0/3, high confidence). This is a consistent and clearly-measured difference, not a borderline call.

Per-assertion results reinforce this: of 24 total assertion checks, with_skill passed 22 (92%) and without_skill passed 3 (12%). Looking at the individual assertions rather than the aggregate:
- Six assertions follow a clean "with_skill passes / without_skill fails" pattern, each with high confidence: stating the reviewed scope, giving findings explicit severity, citing concrete observed values, disclosing what couldn't be checked, giving resource-specific recommendations, and referencing the skill's check identifiers. These are the dimensions actually driving the gap.
- One assertion (no raw 12-digit AWS account IDs exposed) passed for both variants 3/3 — this is a shared strength and does not differentiate the two.
- One assertion ("if no serverless resources exist, say so rather than inventing findings") passed only 1/3 for with_skill and 0/3 for without_skill, and is flagged with low confidence for with_skill — this assertion is weakly measured and shows both variants struggling, suggesting this specific behavior needs further work regardless of variant.

On runtime and cost, with_skill took notably longer (~6m52s vs ~1m28s) and cost more (~$3.43 vs ~$0.73), with higher context-window utilization (18.9% vs 4.7%); neither showed any context compaction. This is a real tradeoff: with_skill's much higher expected-output and assertion pass rates came alongside substantially higher time and cost.

Quality comparison pairs could not be evaluated (0 of 3 pairs compared, all 3 skipped), so no direct quality-preference signal is available beyond the assertion-level data above.

Output consistency across repeated runs differed: with_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.67, high confidence), while without_skill was rated "inconsistent" (score 1.33, high confidence), with without_skill showing "inconsistent" on 2 of 3 dimensions. This suggests without_skill's outputs varied more from run to run, which may partly explain its low expected-output and assertion pass rates.

Overall, the data shows a clear, consistently-measured gap on expected-output match and most assertions favoring with_skill, paired with with_skill using more time, cost, and context budget, and without_skill showing greater run-to-run variability. One assertion (account ID exposure) shows no difference, and one assertion (reporting empty scope) is weakly measured and low-performing for both variants, pointing to a shared gap rather than a differentiator. No formal quality-comparison data was available to weigh in further.

silent-failure-correlation.summary:
Both variants successfully triggered the behavior under test (3/3). From there, the two variants diverge sharply on this eval.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, 100%), with high-confidence judgments and no low-confidence cases. without_skill met the expected output in 0 of 3 runs, also judged with high confidence — so this is a clear, well-supported difference rather than a borderline call.

Per-assertion results: all 15 assertions (5 distinct assertion checks × 3 runs) passed for with_skill and failed for without_skill — a uniform with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails pattern across every assertion, including both LLM-judged criteria (tying failures to specific absent controls, assessing alarm coverage per resource, explaining why findings would go unnoticed, ordering findings with a stated rationale) and a regex-based check (citing the skill's check identifiers). No assertion passed for both variants or failed for both, so none of these assertions are uninformative — each one is discriminating between the two variants in the same direction, which strengthens the overall picture rather than being five independent weak signals.

Quality comparison: this dimension could not be assessed — all 3 pairs were skipped, with 0 pairs actually evaluated, so there is no head-to-head quality judgment to weigh here.

Output consistency: with_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.33, with 1 consistent + 2 mostly-consistent dimension counts, high confidence), while without_skill was rated "inconsistent" across all 3 dimensions checked (score 1.0, high confidence). So without_skill's outputs varied more run-to-run on top of also failing the expected-output and assertion checks.

Metrics show a cost/speed tradeoff in the other direction: without_skill ran faster (avg 2m36s vs 5m35s) and cheaper (avg $1.30 vs $2.79), with lower context-window utilization (5.4% vs 17.1%); neither had any context compaction events. So without_skill used fewer resources and ran faster, but on this eval that efficiency came alongside not meeting the expected output, failing all assertions, and being less consistent across runs.

Overall, this is not a mixed-signal case: expected-output results, every per-assertion check, and output consistency all point the same direction (favoring with_skill's behavior on this particular eval), while without_skill was notably faster and cheaper and quality comparisons were not available to weigh against that. Given the sample size is only 3 runs per variant, these are consistent but still limited-sample findings restricted to this one eval/task.

evidence-and-scope-discipline.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat-task eval run 3 times for each variant. The trigger behavior under test fired reliably in all 3 runs (this metric is only tracked once, not per-variant).

Expected-output match: a stark difference appears here. with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%, high confidence). Since confidence is high on both sides, this gap is a reasonably solid finding rather than a measurement artifact.

Assertion-level detail (18 assertion checks per variant, from 6 distinct assertion types x 3 runs):
- with_skill passed all 18/18 (100%); without_skill passed 5/18 (28%).
- Looking at individual assertion types, one ("No raw 12-digit AWS account IDs are exposed") passed for both variants 3/3 — this check doesn't differentiate the variants.
- Four assertion types show a clear with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails pattern: separating verified vs. unverified checks, not presenting unverified checks as compliant, attributing thresholds to a source, and citing the skill's check identifiers. without_skill failed all of these consistently (0/3 each), while with_skill passed all (3/3 each, high confidence on most, medium on two).
- One assertion (marking cost/savings figures as estimates, or skipping cleanly) was flaky for without_skill (2/3 pass, medium confidence) versus a clean 3/3 for with_skill.
- Overall, the assertion pattern indicates without_skill is missing several specific disclosure/attribution behaviors that with_skill consistently exhibits, though one assertion found no difference at all.

Quality comparison: no quality pairs could actually be evaluated (0 of 3 pairs assessed; all 3 were skipped), so there is no quality-dimension evidence to weigh here — this is an absence of data, not a tie or a loss for either variant.

Runtime and cost: without_skill ran faster (~5m20s vs ~9m25s for with_skill) and cheaper (~$2.66 vs ~$4.69). without_skill also used much less context window (5.2% vs 19.4%); neither variant triggered any compaction. This is a real efficiency difference, but it sits alongside without_skill's much lower rate of meeting expected output and assertions, so it reads as a speed/cost-vs-completeness tradeoff rather than a simple efficiency win.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability): both variants were rated "mostly_consistent" overall, with medium confidence. with_skill scored slightly higher (2.5, with 1 dimension "consistent" and 1 "mostly_consistent") than without_skill (2.0, with 1 "consistent", 1 "mostly_consistent", and 1 "inconsistent" dimension). This suggests without_skill's outputs varied a bit more across repeated runs, though the confidence behind this rating is only medium for both.

Overall picture: the clearest, highest-confidence signal is that with_skill met expected output and nearly all granular assertions (disclosure of verification status, threshold sourcing, check-ID citation) consistently across runs, while without_skill did not — though it did pass one shared assertion and was partially flaky rather than failing outright on another. without_skill was notably faster, cheaper, and used less context, and was slightly more variable run-to-run. No direct quality-judgment comparison was available since all quality pairs were skipped.
